title: Peace of Augsburg
summary: Religious and constitutional settlement of 1555 that recognized Catholic and Lutheran estates within imperial law while leaving several disputed questions unresolved.
why_it_matters: Ferdinand inherits its language as both shield and weapon: enforcing one clause may reassure Catholic petitioners while frightening estates that depend on long local practice.

title: Letter of Majesty
summary: Rudolf II's 1609 Bohemian charter confirming Protestant rights claimed by the Bohemian estates.
why_it_matters: The charter gives Bohemian Protestants a legal language for grievance, while Ferdinand's court can still dispute how far those protections extend.

title: Ferdinand II
summary: Habsburg ruler of Inner Austria, later king of Bohemia, king of Hungary, and emperor.
why_it_matters: The role is built around Ferdinand's attempt to secure dynasty, law, and Catholic restoration without losing the Empire's political cooperation.

title: Inner Austria
summary: The Styrian Habsburg lands of Styria, Carinthia, Krain, Gorz, and Gradisca, lying near the Ottoman frontier and governed by Ferdinand before his imperial rise.
why_it_matters: Ferdinand's successful reform commission in Inner Austria taught him that careful preparation, legal narrowness, Catholic officeholding, and force could restore dynastic authority without immediate general revolt.

title: Cardinal Klesl
summary: Matthias's chief minister and a figure associated with negotiation and dynastic caution during the first Bohemian crisis.
why_it_matters: Keeping or removing him changes whether Ferdinand still has a high-level channel for compromise after Prague.

title: Maximilian of Bavaria
summary: Duke of Bavaria and leader of the Catholic League, indispensable to Ferdinand's early military survival.
why_it_matters: Bavarian help defeats Bohemia, but the price becomes leverage over money, military command, and the Palatine electorate.

title: Treaty of Munich
summary: The 1619 bargain by which Maximilian and the Catholic League supplied decisive aid to Ferdinand under conditions that protected Bavarian interests.
why_it_matters: It turns a survival problem into a dependency problem. Later rewards to Bavaria are not merely generosity; they answer obligations created in the crisis.

title: Frederick V
summary: Elector Palatine, elected king by the Bohemian Confederation in 1619 and later placed under the imperial ban.
why_it_matters: His punishment and possible restoration become a European grievance linking Bohemia, the Palatinate, England, the Dutch, Spain, and Bavaria.

title: John George I of Saxony
summary: Lutheran elector whose legal cooperation helps isolate Bohemia, and whose later alarm helps make Swedish intervention effective.
why_it_matters: Saxony is not simply Protestant opposition. Ferdinand can use Saxon legality, but only while Lutheran trust survives.

title: Albrecht von Wallenstein
summary: Imperial commander and military entrepreneur whose credit, officers, and contribution system gave Ferdinand an army beyond ordinary treasury capacity.
why_it_matters: Wallenstein solves force and finance while creating a power center that can frighten princes, allies, and Vienna itself.

title: Edict of Restitution
summary: Ferdinand's 1629 decree demanding restoration of many ecclesiastical properties and excluding Calvinists from the protection of the religious peace.
why_it_matters: Wilson treats it as a grave overreach: legally framed, confessionally attractive, and politically disastrous among moderate Lutherans.

title: Peace of Lubeck
summary: The 1629 settlement that removed Denmark from the war on comparatively generous terms.
why_it_matters: It offers Ferdinand a chance to convert military success into wider peace, a chance later damaged by restitution politics.

title: Regensburg Electoral Congress
summary: Meetings of electors and imperial authority where consent, succession, military command, and constitutional limits could be bargained.
why_it_matters: Regensburg shows that Ferdinand's imperial title does not give free command; collective politics can force concessions at moments of apparent strength.

title: Peace of Prague
summary: The 1635 imperial settlement with Saxony and many Lutheran estates, compromising on the Edict and reorganizing military authority.
why_it_matters: It can restore much of the Empire to Ferdinand's side, but exclusions from its amnesty keep important enemies in the war.

title: Imperial Ban
summary: A legal punishment placing an offender outside imperial protection and opening the way to confiscation or coercion.
why_it_matters: Against Frederick it strengthens Ferdinand's legal position while turning punishment into a durable Palatine and Protestant grievance.

title: Bohemian Estates
summary: Corporate political bodies of the Bohemian crown lands that claimed privileges, religious protections, and a role in guarding the kingdom's liberties.
why_it_matters: Ferdinand's conflict with them is legal, confessional, dynastic, and constitutional at once; reducing them to rebels or Protestants misses the pressure of the crisis.
